title: Wenzlhuemer, Colonial Systems of Law (British Empire)

slides.title: Common law as the basis of all three types of possession
slides.text: British colonial expansion brought to the newly acquired territories in America, Asia, Africa and the Pacific THE ADMINISTRATION OF ENGLISH COMMON LAW AND STATUTE LAW. Common law had developed in England FROM THE 12TH CENTURY and denoted a body of LARGELY NON-LEGISLATIVE LAW BASED ON CUSTOM AND PRECEDENT; precisely because of that centuries-long development it proved a STABLE AND SLOWLY CHANGING system. It formed the basis of jurisdiction in ALL THREE TYPES OF DIRECT COLONIAL POSSESSION: in the TRADING POSTS along the Indian Ocean coast, in the SETTLER COLONIES of North America, South Africa and Australia, where the settlers brought it with them, and as the legal foundation of ALL BRITISH COLONIES OF DOMINATION in Asia and Africa. Even so, administrators in all three types soon recognised the NEED TO ADAPT THE IMPORTED LAW TO LOCAL CONDITIONS and supplemented English law with COLONIAL STATUTES responding to specific colonial situations.

cards.q: In which types of British possession did common law apply as the foundation?
cards.a: In ALL THREE types of direct possession: in the trading posts along the Indian Ocean, in the settler colonies of North America, South Africa and Australia, and as the legal foundation of all colonies of domination in Asia and Africa. Everywhere, however, it was supplemented by colonial statutes adapted to local conditions.

slides.title: Nonrepugnancy and the Colonial Laws Validity Act 1865
slides.text: UNTIL THE PASSING OF THE COLONIAL LAWS VALIDITY ACT IN 1865, colonial statutes were valid ONLY IN SO FAR AS THEY WERE IN NO RESPECT 'REPUGNANT' TO THE LAW OF THE MOTHER COUNTRY. And now beware of the usual misunderstanding: although the Act is often criticised for embodying the principle of NONREPUGNANCY, IT IN FACT RECOGNISED COLONIAL LEGISLATION AND DECLARED REPUGNANT STATUTES VOID ONLY TO THE EXTENT OF THEIR REPUGNANCY to British law — whereas previously they had been void IN THEIR ENTIRETY. The Act and the principle of nonrepugnancy governed colonial legislation IN ALL BRITISH POSSESSIONS, REGARDLESS OF COLONIAL SELF-GOVERNMENT, until the STATUTE OF WESTMINSTER OF 1931, which gave validity to every statute passed by a dominion parliament. In the crown colonies the Colonial Laws Validity Act applied UNTIL INDEPENDENCE.

terms.def: The principle that a colonial statute must not be repugnant to the law of the mother country. From 1865 only with partial invalidity to the extent of the repugnancy, not invalidity of the whole statute.

cards.q: What did the Colonial Laws Validity Act 1865 actually do?
cards.a: It recognised the validity of colonial legislation and declared repugnant statutes void ONLY TO THE EXTENT OF THEIR REPUGNANCY to British law — whereas previously they had been void IN THEIR ENTIRETY. Despite its reputation, it therefore rather strengthened the colonial legislature.

cards.q: How long did the principle of nonrepugnancy apply, and what ended it?
cards.a: It applied in all British possessions REGARDLESS OF COLONIAL SELF-GOVERNMENT until the STATUTE OF WESTMINSTER OF 1931, which gave validity to every statute passed by a dominion parliament. In the crown colonies it applied until independence.

slides.title: Trading posts: consular law and creeping extension
slides.text: When the European trading companies began to establish posts in territories under foreign sovereignty, they made use of a practice widespread among the merchant companies of the day — CONSULAR LAW. Local rulers, especially in Asia, recognised THE RIGHT OF FOREIGN MERCHANTS TO LIVE UNDER THEIR OWN LEGAL ORDER, in order to encourage and protect foreign trade. In this way the BRITISH EAST INDIA COMPANY brought English law to its factories in India; its FOUNDING CHARTER OF 1600 already referred indirectly to the principle of nonrepugnancy as regards laws and punishments in the company's future territories. The company's legal authority was vested in MINIATURE GOVERNMENTS and originally COVERED ONLY BRITISH SUBJECTS. In 1661 legal authority over the company's servants and other Europeans passed to the GOVERNOR AND COUNCIL. But as the company's power in the trading posts grew, IT EXTENDED ITS JURISDICTION TO CASES BETWEEN EUROPEANS AND NATIVES AND FINALLY ASSUMED LEGAL AUTHORITY OVER THE NATIVE POPULATION AS WELL. Native cases, however, were as a rule decided by LOCAL JUDGES ACCORDING TO LOCAL CUSTOMARY LAW — and thus a practice of LEGAL PLURALISM became established.

cards.q: How did consular law turn into rule over the native population?
cards.a: The East India Company's legal authority originally covered only British subjects (from 1661 other Europeans too, in the hands of the governor and council), but as its power grew it extended its jurisdiction to cases between Europeans and natives and finally assumed legal authority over the native population. Native cases, however, were decided by local judges under local customary law — hence legal pluralism.

slides.title: Settler colonies: law as a white privilege
slides.text: In territories with a relatively sparse native population and permanent European immigration, the settlers claimed English common law and statute law AS THE SOLE AND EXCLUSIVE LAW OF THE NEW COLONIES. TO LIVE UNDER ENGLISH LAW WAS UNDERSTOOD AS A PRIVILEGE RESERVED TO THE WHITE POPULATION, and there was no willingness to share it with the natives. The highest legal authority in civil and criminal matters was the GOVERNOR AND COUNCIL, appointed by the king or (in chartered colonies) by the proprietor. In theory they were bound by the principle of nonrepugnancy, but SLOW COMMUNICATION AND THE PRACTICE OF ENACTING 'TEMPORARY' LAWS guaranteed them considerable legislative latitude. Adaptation to local conditions took concrete form: in the North American colonies THE IMPORT OF AFRICAN SLAVES required EUROPEAN-DESIGNED STATUTES GOVERNING THE RELATION OF MASTER AND SLAVE; in the Australian settlements the colonists adopted the practice of TERRA NULLIUS, thereby refusing to recognise native claims to land and securing European titles. Settler colonies rarely produced legal pluralisms (and where they did, in the weakest form) — THEY CONFIRMED BRITISH LAW AS THE ONLY LEGAL SYSTEM. And an essential point: SELF-GOVERNMENT IN THE SETTLER COLONIES DID NOT OVERRIDE THE PRINCIPLE OF NONREPUGNANCY; only by the Statute of Westminster did the six British dominions (Australia, Canada, the Irish Free State, New Zealand, Newfoundland and South Africa) obtain FULL LEGAL AUTHORITY.

cards.q: Why did settler colonies not produce legal pluralism?
cards.a: Because the settlers claimed English law as the SOLE law of the colony, and to live under it was understood as a PRIVILEGE reserved to the white population, which they did not share with the natives. The law was adapted to local conditions (slave statutes in North America, terra nullius in Australia) but remained the only system.

cards.q: Did self-government in the settler colonies override the principle of nonrepugnancy?
cards.a: NO. Full legal authority was obtained by the six British dominions — Australia, Canada, the Irish Free State, New Zealand, Newfoundland and South Africa — only by the Statute of Westminster in 1931. Until then it was slow communication and the practice of 'temporary' laws, rather than legal standing, that gave the governor and council their latitude.

slides.title: India: from Hastings to codification
slides.text: WITH THE ACQUISITION OF BENGAL IN 1757 the East India Company (and with it the British government) faced the new task of administering law for European and native subjects alike. The legal pluralism familiar from the factories was established by the LEGAL REFORMS OF WARREN HASTINGS (1732–1818), the first Governor-General of India, IN 1772: MUSLIMS UNDER MUSLIM CIVIL LAW, HINDUS UNDER HINDU CIVIL LAW, AND ALL NATIVES UNDER MUSLIM CRIMINAL LAW. To this was added the REGULATING ACT 1773, which extended British jurisdiction to all British subjects, all servants of the company and all other natives who VOLUNTARILY SUBMITTED to it. The British began to interfere in the native legal orders ONLY IN THE SECOND QUARTER OF THE 19TH CENTURY, when they discovered India's economic value beyond the collection of taxes. AFTER THE INDIAN REBELLION OF 1857 THE BRITISH CROWN TOOK OVER THE INDIAN POSSESSIONS FROM THE COMPANY IN 1858. In 1860 a UNIFORM INDIAN PENAL CODE was introduced, and by the end of the century most commercial, criminal and procedural law was FULLY CODIFIED — WITH VERY LITTLE NATIVE LEGAL PRACTICE INCORPORATED. Legal pluralism survived only in HINDU AND MUSLIM PERSONAL LAW. And the point: AFTER INDEPENDENCE IN 1947 THE LEGAL ORDER ESTABLISHED BY THE BRITISH REMAINED PRACTICALLY UNTOUCHED.

cards.q: What did Hastings's reforms of 1772 introduce?
cards.a: Legal pluralism by religion: Muslims under Muslim civil law, Hindus under Hindu civil law — but ALL NATIVES under MUSLIM CRIMINAL LAW. The Regulating Act 1773 then extended British jurisdiction to British subjects, servants of the company and those natives who voluntarily submitted to it.

cards.q: What became of Indian legal pluralism in the 19th century?
cards.a: After the rebellion of 1857 the crown took over the possessions in 1858; in 1860 came the uniform INDIAN PENAL CODE, and by the end of the century most commercial, criminal and procedural law was fully codified with minimal native practice. Pluralism survived only in HINDU AND MUSLIM PERSONAL LAW — and after independence in 1947 the British order remained practically untouched.

slides.title: India as a model, and indirect rule
slides.text: The practice developed in colonial India became the MODEL FOR THE OTHER BRITISH COLONIES OF DOMINATION. The accepted practice became: CODIFICATION, THE EXTENSION OF BRITISH LAW AND THE APPLICATION OF NATIVE CUSTOMARY LAW IN PERSONAL MATTERS. Under the name INDIRECT RULE the British used NATIVE ELITES TO ADMINISTER LAW in their African colonies and thus maintained a certain form of legal pluralism. But — and this is the sentence to have ready: LOCAL CUSTOMARY LAWS MOSTLY SURVIVED ONLY IN ALTERED FORMS AS APPENDAGES OF BRITISH STATE LAW.

terms.def: British administration of law in the African colonies through native elites — it preserved the form of legal pluralism, but customary laws survived only as altered appendages of British state law.

cards.q: What is indirect rule and what happened to customary law under it?
cards.a: British administration of law in the African colonies through NATIVE ELITES, which maintained the form of legal pluralism. Local customary laws, however, mostly survived ONLY IN ALTERED FORMS AS APPENDAGES OF BRITISH STATE LAW.

slides.title: What colonial law was for
slides.text: The author's summary, and it is merciless: THE PRIMARY PURPOSE OF COLONIAL LAW WAS TO SECURE THE INTERESTS OF THE COLONISERS. British statutes on LAND AND PROPERTY secured British acquisition of land and title to it in the settler colonies and later INVESTMENT IN PLANTATIONS. British-designed SLAVE STATUTES governed the relation of master and slave in North America and secured a STEADY AND RELIABLE LABOUR FORCE. In the trading posts British law on a consular basis guaranteed PERSONAL SECURITY IN A FOREIGN SOCIETY AND PROTECTED FOREIGN TRADE. In settler and non-settler colonies alike, to fall under British jurisdiction was understood as a PRIVILEGE which there was no willingness to share with the natives — and THE RESULTING LEGAL PLURALISM MAINTAINED LEGAL INEQUALITY IN THE NON-SETTLER COLONIES. The codification of colonial law, into which altered forms of local customary law were incorporated, ultimately IMPOSED ON MANY COLONIES OF DOMINATION A EUROPEANISED LEGAL SYSTEM, much of which remained in force INTO THE POST-COLONIAL PERIOD AS WELL.

cards.q: What was colonial law for — list by type of possession.
cards.a: To secure the interests of the colonisers. Land and property statutes secured the acquisition of land and title in the settler colonies and later plantation investment; slave statutes secured a steady labour force in North America; and in the trading posts British law on a consular basis guaranteed personal security and the protection of trade.

cards.q: What was the relation between legal pluralism and equality in the colonies?
cards.a: Legal pluralism MAINTAINED LEGAL INEQUALITY IN THE NON-SETTLER COLONIES — it followed from the fact that falling under British jurisdiction was a privilege not shared with the natives. And codification, which absorbed altered customary law, then imposed a Europeanised system that survived decolonisation.
